item.content:encoded:
A glass-walled pavilion sandwiched between historic buildings is the leading feature of an Oregon art museum revamp, which was designed by US studios Hennebery Eddy Architects and Vinci Hamp Architects to improve the visitor experience.

Spanning two urban blocks, the Portland Art Museum is located in the city's downtown district.

It primarily consists of two historic buildings: the Belluschi Building, designed by architect Pietro Belluschi and completed in 1932, and the Mark Building, designed by Frederick Fritsch and dating to 1926. The latter originally served as a masonic temple and was acquired by the museum in the 1990s.

Local studio Hennebery Eddy Architects and Chicago-based Vinci Hamp Architects were tasked with updating the museum's existing buildings and adding a connector building – with the overall goal to provide a "more streamlined and holistic visitor experience".

For the connector building, the team conceived the Mark Rothko Pavilion, named after the abstract expressionist artist who grew up in Portland.

The multi-storey, 24,000-square-foot (223-square-metre) structure sits between the two historic buildings.

"The pavilion establishes a new main entry and links previously discontinuous circulation and disparate floor elevations, creating an intuitive and cohesive venue for art," the team said.

Rather than a simple box, the pavilion has setbacks that give it a more dynamic look. Along one side, the team cut away a portion of the ground level to form a breezeway for pedestrians and cyclists.

"The passageway connects the east and west entry plazas, where key pieces from the museum's sculpture collection are accessible to the public, establishing a uniquely Portland feature that offers passersby sheltered views into galleries and extends the museum experience into the public realm," the team said.

Designed to respect the context, the pavilion has glazed walls lined with long, metal mullions and white-ceramic frit.

These elements are a nod to the historic neighbours – specifically the travertine trim found on the Belluschi Building and the vertical elements that characterise the Mark Building.

"The crystalline, contemporary form of the Rothko Pavilion projects a distinctly modernist character but respects its historic partners," the team said.

Within the pavilion, extensive glazing provides a connection to the surrounding neighbourhood. A restrained material palette includes white oak flooring in galleries and granite pavers in other areas.

The pavilion's ground level contains the museum's Community Commons, which is free to enter and was conceived "as a gathering space for all".

Upper-level terraces offer visitors the chance "to step outside and take in Portland's skyline and iconic South Park Blocks", the latter a reference to a 12-block stretch of green space.

In addition to the new Rothko Pavilion, the museum project also included renovations to the existing structures, with a focus on improving the galleries in a way that "puts art first".

In the Belluschi Building, traditional-style galleries have been refreshed. The team also added a volume that holds an upper-floor gallery and a receiving dock on the lower level.

Within the Mark Building, the team "simplified" the galleries and updated an auditorium.

Read:

Vacant supermarket in Portland converted into library facility by Hennebery Eddy

It also converted a library into a 2,700-square-foot (251-square-metre) gallery dedicated to contemporary work by emerging artists. The library was moved to another part of the building.

The project also entailed a revamp of the museum's cafe, store, and spaces for the conservation and education departments.

Overall, the renovation and expansion have greatly improved the visitor experience and solved challenges that have plagued the museum for decades, according to the team.

"The $111 million expansion is one of the most significant capital investments in the arts in the history of Oregon," the team said.

"The updated campus balances the needs of its urban neighbourhood and the city and reinforces the museum's role as a cultural beacon of downtown Portland."

Other recent projects in Portland include the conversion of a vacant supermarket into a library facility by Hennebery Eddy and a ZGF-designed expansion of the main terminal at Portland International Airport, which features a giant mass-timber roof.

item.content:encoded:
Plans unveiled by architecture studio Buckley Gray Yeoman for offices, homes and a data centre near Brick Lane in London have been approved.

Planned for three sites in the east London neighbourhood, the Truman Brewery masterplan will comprise eight buildings designed by Buckley Gray Yeoman (BGY), alongside London-based studios Carmody Groarke, Morris+Company and Henley Halebrown.

Approved last week by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, the contentious proposal will include a 5,200-square-metre data centre designed by Morris+Company.

Additionally, plans for 35,000-square-metres of office, retail and community space will include the redevelopment of the existing Truman Brewery. This will see a two-story extension and public space added to the building's grade II-listed Boiler House.

Forty four homes will also be built as part of the development, six of which will be social housing specifically designed to accommodate larger Bangladeshi-heritage families.

Renders of the proposal reveal a series of multi-storey buildings flanked by courtyards and signposted by the Truman Brewery chimney.

Plans originally submitted by BGY in 2024 were strongly opposed by the Tower Hamlets Council and local campaign group Save Brick Lane, which argued the development could displace local residents and businesses.

Despite controversy over the plans, the UK Housing Secretary Angela Rayner suggested that the Truman Brewery proposal will bring "increased footfall" to local businesses and generate employment.

Rayner and Labour minister Matthew Pennycook also praised the data centre for its "very significant" public benefits and "associated economic benefits".

Read:

Images of relocated London Museum by Stanton Williams and Asif Khan revealed

In response to the approved plans, Save Brick Lane expressed that it was "deeply disappointed".

Tower Hamlets mayor Lutfur Rahman also criticised the lack of social housing, noting a "missed opportunity" to address the borough's "acute housing crisis", according to the BBC.

"Against that backdrop, development of this scale delivering only six homes for social rent falls significantly short of addressing local need," Rahman said.

In other architecture news, plug-in solar panels, which can be fitted onto balconies, are set to become available in the UK and the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard has been launched by certification company Bureau Veritas in a bid to minimise greenwashing.

The renders are by Conica Studio.

item.content:encoded:
Irregularly placed and mismatched openings puncture the terracotta-toned, double-layered exterior of 100 Windows, a multigenerational home in Vietnam designed by local architecture practice Inrestudio.

Designed for two generations and three households – a couple, their two sons and the sons' families – the 639-square-metre home is located close to the Red River in the suburbs of Hanoi.

Responding to both the region's tropical climate and the likelihood of extensive development in the future, Inrestudio wrapped the home with a double-layered exterior to create pockets of private outdoor space and help filter air through its interiors.

"The project is shaped around ambiguity," studio founder Niko told Dezeen. "The suburb itself is ambiguous, neither city nor countryside, and so is its future; even 'family' is an ambiguous unit here, three households whose composition will keep changing,"

"As a vessel for this indeterminate program, an abstract house form retains a minimal symbol of 'house', while the many openings set the building apart from its neighbours," he added.

While the home features multiple windows, its name 100 Windows was intended "as a symbolic expression of abundance, rather than a literal count of one hundred windows," Niko said.

The home is elevated atop a slightly setback base of dark, textured concrete. A floor paved in basalt unites an external patio with a swimming pool and the ground floor living, dining and kitchen areas.

Above, two storeys of bedrooms and a top floor with a second living, dining and kitchen area have been designed to adapt to a variety of family arrangements, with the whole being encased within the home's distinctive double-skin facade.

Read:

Perforated brick wall fronts breezy home in Vietnam by Live Out Studio

Numerous openings puncture both layers of this facade. Many of these openings align to give the home's windows unobstructed views, while some have been offset to provide shade and privacy to recessed balconies and thin terraces.

Inrestudio also used the additional thickness of this double-layered exterior to create shelving, desks, storage and ventilation channels that help to cool the interiors, which have been finished with dark timber floors and exposed concrete ceilings.

"The plan is kept as generic as possible so it can accept many futures, and the 'loose double skin' sustains a relationship with the surroundings that can stay open and diverse over a long time," Niko said.

"Life does not complete itself at the centre of the house but seeps out toward its edges. These in-between places have no proper names, but they are where people gather and time is well spent," he continued.

"This richness of the periphery is something an urban house cannot afford; in the countryside it is not needed, because a generous exterior is already there. Securing richness at the edge of the building itself is, to us, a very suburban act."

The rooftop living area of 100 Windows opens out onto a large terrace, which sits beneath an open grid of terracotta-toned concrete beams that is angled to continue the slope of the home's roof.

Other homes in Vietnam recently featured on Dezeen include an extension by ODDO Architects informed by Hanoi's narrow alleyways, and a home in Da Nang by Live Out Studio that is fronted by a perforated brick wall.

The photography is by Trieu Chien.

item.content:encoded:
Work has begun on the demolition of the never-opened Rike Concert Hall in Tbilisi, which was designed by Italian practice Studio Fuksas.

Local news organisation TV Pirveli filmed the cladding being removed from the Rike Concert Hall in central Tbilisi last week.

The work began less than two weeks after the Tbilisi city hall architecture department issued a permit allowing the building's owner to demolish the concert hall.

Designed by Studio Fuksas, the building in the central Rike Park has remained empty and closed since 2012, when it was largely complete.

The building was built as part of a rejuvenation plan for the city enacted under previous president Mikheil Saakashvili.

Georgia's change of government in 2012 is largely seen as the reason the project was abandoned, with the concert hall connected to the previous regime.

The extremely distinctive building consists of two tube-shaped volumes that open out onto the riverside park. Each of the tubes was covered in square stainless-steel panels that resemble scales.

In the news report published by TV Pirveli last week, a video was captured showing these cladding panels being removed and the structure underneath exposed.

Read:

Planned demolition of Tbilisi concert hall "a significant cultural setback" says Studio Fuksas

The demolition has begun less than 15 years after construction of the building's structure was largely complete, although the internal fit-out never happened.

After a decade of closure, the building was sold to a property developer in 2022, who in turn sold it to the current owner – Makro Constructions – in 2025.

Following news of the planned demolition last month, Studio Fuksas described the plans as "a significant cultural setback". In a statement to Dezeen, it claimed that the studio had received no response to efforts to contact the local government.

"Over the past months, the studio repeatedly offered to work with the Georgian authorities to explore alternative solutions that could preserve and repurpose this iconic building, avoiding what we believe would be a premature and irreversible demolition," said the studio.

"Unfortunately, these proposals have received no response."

The photography is courtesy of Studio Fuksas.

item.content:encoded:
Scottish architect Ruairidh Moir has launched a campaign to rebuild the fire-torn Mackintosh Building at the Glasgow School of Art, calling on "an independent body to own and take forward the project".

The campaign calls for the building's ownership to be transferred to an independent organisation to deliver a "faithful restoration and reinstatement". It also asks the Scottish and UK governments for financial assistance.

At the time of writing, it has 5,406 signatures. The target is 100,000, at which stage the petition will be "hand-delivered" to both Scottish and UK Governments and the board of Glasgow School of Art (GSA).

The campaign follows GSA's recent announcement that it cannot afford to rebuild the iconic Mackintosh Building, known affectionately as The Mack, without external funding.

Moir, a conservation architect and founder of Glasgow studio BARD, said he initiated the petition to "reflect the views of many people who have cared deeply about the school for years".

"We owe it to Charles Rennie Mackintosh"

"There has been frustration at the GSA's stewardship of the building, both before the fires and in the years that have followed," Moir told Dezeen.

"The recent statements by the School of Art governors have galvanised many to step forward and unite to remove the obstructions and demonstrate support for Mackintosh's masterpiece," he continued.

The fire-torn art school is the best-known building designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh, Scotland's most famous architect.

A fire ripped through the building in 2014, before a second and more destructive fire occurred during a £35 million restoration project in 2018.

Shortly after the second blaze, the former director of the GSA Tom Inns said that it would be rebuilt. But restoration works are now on hold.

In Moir's view, it needs to be rebuilt as "it is genuinely one of the finest achievements of architecture".

"The Mack must be rebuilt because it is so important. Architecture of such renowned and recognised quality is not that common. This one sits amongst the very highest tier of architectural achievement and is beloved," he explained.

"We owe it to Charles Rennie Mackintosh, Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh, Fra Newbery, and to all those who have loved the building; to our culture and heritage; and to our sense of self, to get this right for Scotland and for the world."

GSA has "continually failed"

While the campaign calls for the ownership of the building to be transferred, it also states the building should be made available "on a lease-back arrangement to GSA" to make sure it can remain as an art school.

Moir added that a panel of experts would need to be created to advise a new design and project team.

"The need for an independent body to own and take forward the project, protecting it for future generations, is borne out by the fact that the GSA board has continually failed to deliver it," explained Moir.

"There is understandably little confidence in allowing the body that has failed Mackintosh's masterpiece in this way to have a third attempt. Time for a fresh start."

For Moir, the thought of the school being left as a ruin "leaves [him] cold".

While there is also always a risk of pastiche in reconstruction work, the architect believes it can be achieved to the same quality as the original.

Read:

Glasgow School of Art "cannot rebuild" Mackintosh Building

"There are huge challenges in achieving it, but the will, finance, client, leadership and skills all need to be there for a successful outcome," he said. "We cannot allow incompatible or phoney materials to be used; it must be authentic to the way Mackintosh left it for us to care for."

"Few buildings are as comprehensively recorded as the School of Art. Backing away from a full and faithful reinstatement because of loose arguments around pastiche or authenticity would, in my view, be a profound mistake. We have almost everything at our fingertips to faithfully reinstate the building."

Since GSA's announcement, many industry figures have spoken out with views similar to Moir. Among them was British designer Thomas Heatherwick, who compared the need to rebuild to Notre-Dame Cathedral.

"To accept a diminished future for it would show a worrying lack of cultural confidence," he wrote in an Instagram post shared by Humanise.

"When Notre-Dame burned, Paris didn't shrug and scale down its ambition. It responded with imagination, leadership and national will. Paris came out stronger afterwards," he said.

"Let's all urge the Scottish Government, Glasgow City Council, businesses, funders, cultural leaders and communities to work together with GSA to find a way to restore the Mackintosh Building with the care, seriousness and ambition it deserves."

item.content:encoded:
Plans for a large new building in Rotterdam intended to encourage people to lead more environmentally friendly lifestyles are wrong-headed and should be scrapped in a blaze of publicity, writes Barnabas Calder.

Putting plants on a building doesn't make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan. Yet image searches for "sustainable architecture" puke out a page of gas-guzzling big new buildings with greenery on their walls or balconies.

Dutch architecture studio MVRDV has won a competition with a new specimen of plant-washing, the Shift Embassy. Let's hope it remains unbuilt.

The client, social enterprise Shift, declares that "a fossil-fuel-based economy built on the unsustainable myth of perpetual economic growth [is] leading us toward ecological and social catastrophe." True, and each summer the proof obtrudes itself in longer, hotter heatwaves, bigger wildfires and worsening crop failures.

I would be happy for it to look considerably worse if it were less harmful environmentally

The Shift Embassy, also called "Rotterdam Rocks!", is a bizarre response to the organisation's anti-growth stance: a 200-bed hotel, posh restaurant, offices, and a 5,000-square-metre exhibition space for attracting international tourists to Rotterdam, in the hope that once they are there they will think hard enough about sustainability to go home and change their lives.

Its aesthetics are attracting the usual derision that clusters round different-looking buildings – comparisons with the Flintstones, with faeces and with genitalia. The same practice's Marble Arch Mound showed how hard it can be to make urban vegetation schemes convincing.

Looks, though, seem a trivial concern in the face of ecological catastrophe. I would be happy for it to look considerably worse if it were less harmful environmentally.

Read:

MVRDV wins competition for "new world wonder" in the Netherlands

The "rock-like" surfaces of the architects' press release turn out, on some more clicking around, to be concrete. MVRDV promises "low-carbon concrete", but if that's a matter of swapping cement for industrial co-products such as GGBS the benefits for emissions may be negligible at best. As the Institution of Structural Engineers warns, the supply of GGBS is already almost at capacity, so trucking it in for this building likely means another project will miss out, and have to use normal higher-carbon cement instead.

The engineering relies on reclaimed steel. Reusing a beam is often better than melting it down, but again, if not reclaimed for this project the same steel would be either reclaimed or recycled for another project. Around 70 per cent of all steel still comes from ore, with recycling and reclamation already using most scrap steel. Reclaimed steel is, in other words, also no magic bullet for decarbonisation.

There are some good initiatives in the proposal. The exhibition area will be allowed a certain latitude of temperature variation across the year, as opposed to the offices, hotel and restaurant, which require "high-quality indoor environments" – code, presumably, for the uncomfortably excessive cooling of most commercial interiors in summer, and overbearing heating during winter.

The message given by the building as a whole is wrong

The restaurant will be plant-based. Shift also aims to grow as much greenery as it can around the building. If you really must build a new building, a wider temperature range, extensive planting and meat-free catering are good measures.

There is a welcome honesty to the way Shift discusses the downsides of an "iconic" new building. Its argument is that by influencing visitors' future behaviour, "the societal impact is estimated to be 10,000 times greater than the environmental impact associated with the building's construction and energy use".

This figure assumes that over 50 years, 20 per cent of 25,000,000 projected visitors will lastingly drop two tonnes per year from their personal carbon footprint as a result of the visit.

Read:

"It's time to see all those circular economy strategies for what they are"

But even if that figure proves robust, what about the societal impact of the architecture itself? Unfortunately, the more successfully Shift establishes itself in the minds of a wide international public as a leader in sustainability, the more harm its building can do.

Whatever nuanced analysis Shift conducts of the qualities and problems tied to experimenting with low-carbon materials, the message given by the building as a whole is wrong. It supports the myth that sustainable architecture means new, tall concrete and steel buildings with lifts and powerful air-treatment systems, but some plants on them.

Shift acknowledges that retrofitting an existing building would have been more sustainable, but says there was no suitable candidate in the big new Waterkant development its embassy will be part of. Instead, the organisation ran a major architecture competition for something new, dense and iconic – a brief that could only realistically be executed with profoundly unsustainable materials and methods, and that depends thereafter on millions of tourists flying round the world in environmentally destructive pursuit of distraction and novelty.

If Shift now abandons this project in a blaze of publicity it will do immense good

This is not the degrowth that Shift calls for, but it's not too late to fix things. If Shift now abandons this project in a blaze of publicity, explaining that the environmental cost is too high – an example of outdated and profoundly unsustainable architectural thinking – it will do immense good, and will demonstrate a profound and inspiring commitment to degrowth.

Should that lose the organisation some funding, so be it. Maximising income, investment and capital expenditure is not a degrowth approach.

Shift's own estimates of the good its building will do are based on pilot activities where it reports participants dropped their emissions by an average of 30 per cent. Why not spend the reported €240,000,000 that the building will cost delivering more of these remarkably effective pilot activities instead?

Read:

Can we quit our air-con addiction?

That would save the 15,000 tonnes of carbon-dioxide-equivalent emissions that it reports will be required to produce and power the MVRDV building over 50 years, and the 35,000,000 tonnes it assumes will be emitted as a result of people travelling there. More importantly, though, Shift could push back against architecture's devastating environmental harms by setting such a powerful, well-evidenced example of having the courage not to go ahead with an avoidable building project.

At present, the construction industry and the running of buildings together amount to 37 per cent of global carbon emissions. The most inspirational thing that any architecture practice or client can do is to radically opt out of this harm: make brilliant use of what's already here; tweak and improve in modest, impactful ways; spread the word about the immense ecological harms done by our making and running new buildings.

Shift has the chance to be the ambassador for a real shift – a shift to understanding that sustainable architecture means a new wooden shutter on an old window, not a big bulk of concrete, steel and HVAC peeping out guiltily from behind a leafy toupée.

Barnabas Calder is head of the History of Architecture Research Cluster at the University of Liverpool, and author of Architecture: From Prehistory To Climate Emergency (2021) and Raw Concrete: The Beauty of Brutalism (2016).

item.content:encoded:
Exhibitions Architecture's Inscriptions, Maggie's: Architecture That Cares and Wellbeing in the City are among the architecture and design events featured in Dezeen Events Guide this August.

Other events taking place during the month include Helsinki Design Week, Jia Curated and The Art-Marotte Masterclass Series.

Maggie's: Architecture That Cares
6 March to 1 November, UK

Presented at the V&A Dundee, Maggie's: Architecture That Cares is an exhibition celebrating the architecture behind UK-based charity Maggie's.

The exhibition features models of the cancer care centres, including work by architects Norman Foster, Frank Gehry, Zaha Hadid,  Richard Rogers and Benedetta Tagliabue.

Wellbeing in the City
24 April to 20 September, Spain

The Wellbeing in the City exhibition explores how traditional architecture has impacted the biological, social and spatial experiences of people living in urban spaces.

The display outlines eight key elements of impact, including birth, nurturing, eating, healing, sleeping, playing, courting and walking.

The showcase is curated by architecture practice Izaskun Chinchilla and takes place at La Arquería de Nuevos Ministerios in Madrid.

Architecture's Inscriptions
9 July to 7 October, China

This exhibition demonstrates the influence ancient manuscripts, calligraphy, scholar's rocks, paintings and rubbings have on the work of contemporary Chinese architects.

Architects Huang Wenjing, Li Hu, Liu Jiakun, Liu Yichun, Zhang Ke, Zhu Xiaofeng and Zhuang Shen and artists Ding Yi, Xu Bing and Zhan Wang are all taking part in Architecture's Inscriptions, which takes place at Tank Shanghai.

Jia Curated
13 to 17 August, Indonesia

Jia Curated is an annual design, craft and culture festival taking place in Bali, welcoming over 250 brands across the fields of art, architecture, materiality, landscape design and construction.

This year's event will follow the theme Nature Weave, addressing "interwoven relationships" between people and nature, and the impact on design and craft, such as biophilia practices.

The Art-Marotte Masterclass Series
17 to 21 August, Belgium

A five-day workshop programme will take place at Château Art-Marotte in Braives, Belgium, inviting postgraduate students to experiment with ceramics and materiality.

The masterclass series will offer students the experience to develop their skills in ceramic screen printing and sculpture, using materials such as slumped glass and plaster.

Helsinki Design Week
28 August to 6 September, Finland

Helsinki Design Week celebrates its 21st anniversary in August with the theme The Oncoming Other, spotlighting community, collaboration and connection in urban space.

The programme of exhibitions, talks and open showrooms explores a range of disciplines, including textile, product, industrial, fashion, interior and graphic design.

About Dezeen Events Guide

Dezeen Events Guide is our guide to the best architecture and design events taking place across the world each year. The guide is updated weekly and includes virtual events, conferences, trade fairs, major exhibitions and design weeks.

Inclusion in the guide is free for basic listings, with events selected at Dezeen's discretion. Organisers can get standard, enhanced or featured listings for their events, including images, additional text and links, by paying a modest fee.

In addition, events can ensure inclusion by partnering with Dezeen. For more details on inclusion in Dezeen Events Guide and media partnerships with Dezeen, email eventsguide@dezeen.com.

item.content:encoded:
The UK government has announced the arrival of plug-in solar panels that can be fitted onto balconies to reduce household energy costs.

Expected to be sold in UK stores before the end of summer, the low-cost panels, which are already widely used across Europe, connect directly to a mains socket and can be placed on balconies, roofs or any outdoor space without installation.

Following an announcement by the government in March, recent changes to existing plug and electricity safety regulations in the UK will allow the use of these plug-in solar devices from 27th August.

The new legislation means that UK households, including flat owners and renters, will be able to generate their own electricity and cut energy bills.

New legislation "a major win" for UK households

"Seeing these systems available in stores by summer would be a major win for households, enabling people to take advantage of the longer, brighter days and start generating their own clean electricity straight away," head of UK communications for EcoFlow Lorna Wallace-Smith said.

"For many households – particularly those living in flats or rented homes – solar has not always been straightforward. Plug-and-play systems remove that barrier, making it far easier to get started," Wallace-Smith added.

Read:

New homes in England to have bird-friendly swift bricks in planning reform

The move, which was published under the Starmer Labour government, is part of a wider clean energy initiative that aims to reduce the UK's dependency on global fossil fuel markets as energy costs soar amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Solar panels to become standard for new homes

Alongside the legislation, new rules for the Future Homes Standard are set to come into force next March, mandating low-carbon heating and on-site solar panels for the majority of new homes.

According to the government, these new measures could reportedly save households up to £830 a year on energy bills, as well as create 75 per cent less carbon emissions than homes built to the 2013 standards.

"The Future Homes Standard is a landmark moment for clean energy in Britain," Energy UK's chief executive Dhara Vyas said.

"New homes built under this standard will benefit from clean heating solutions and solar, protecting households from volatile gas prices and putting energy security within the home itself," Vyas added.

Other recent sustainability initiatives in the UK include policy changes to the National Planning Policy Framework requiring new builds to be fitted with bird-friendly swift bricks.

Meanwhile, in the US, the American Institute of Architects has "celebrated" a recently passed bill aimed at speeding up the building and access of affordable housing in the country.

item.content:encoded:
Brooklyn-based Studio Vural has renovated a loft apartment inside a former herring canning factory in New York's West Village, adding tonal green accents throughout.

Studio Vural overhauled the loft within a 1920s building on Barrow Street, which dates back to the era when the West Village was an industrial port.

"Starting with the Vita Herring Factory, our design unveils layers of architectural history and creates a new chapter by contemporising historic elements," studio founder Selim Vural told Dezeen.

"On the exact same concrete slab of an iconic building, a new family, a new life, a new architecture come into being."

The building was converted into co-op residences in the late 1980s by architect Cy Winthrop, who resided in this apartment.

"[Winthrop's] labour of love completely obscured the original structure with smoky mirrored walls, laminate everything and a small koi pond in a corner of the living room," said studio founder Selim Vural.

Stripping all of these elements back, apart from a few unique details, the team was able to unveil a layered history of the building while incorporating new additions.

"We exposed the original concrete columns and beams and managed to save the 80s parquet floors and (some) cabinetry," said Vural. "We added contemporary elements such as earthy cement tiles, acoustic felt panels and glass blocks in warm wood."

The brief was to create an open space for hosting parties, with three flexible bedrooms and a private primary suite.

Squeezing all of these elements into the 1,500-square-foot (139-square-metre) space proved challenging, so the team had to play with their proportions, scale and positions in order to fit.

"We think of the layout as 'pods in a box' with a home office/flex bedroom, a loft reading area and a sleeping nook nestled in a large shell," said Studio Vural.

These pods are wrapped in oak and lit via spandrel windows and large glass blocks.

Green felt was used to cover concrete ceiling beams above the lofted area, as well as the treads and risers of the stairs used to reach it.

Opposite, the kitchen also features oak millwork, while a dining table nestled against a custom built-in seat can accommodate eight.

Read:

Studio Vural reinterprets Japanese interiors for Warren Street Townhouse

The living area beyond features more bespoke furniture that faces a green-painted wall and tiled fireplace.

Behind this wall is the primary bedroom, which is neutrally decorated and includes plenty of built-in storage.

The green and oak colour combination reappears in the bathrooms, where tiles in various verdant tones clad the walls inside the shower and around the vanities.

All of these elements interplay with the original concrete and metal columns, some of which are tucked away while others are more visible.

Studio Vural has previously renovated a townhouse in Brooklyn using Kyoto merchant houses as a reference point, and also imagined a Manhattan tower draped in colourful flowers and an off-the-grid Dune House for Cape Cod.

Other West Village residences that have received an upgrade include a duplex apartment in which a "garden folly" was inserted and a home that was transformed into a show space for contemporary art and design.

item.content:encoded:
French studio PCA-Stream has completed La Source Vive, a domed copper-clad concert hall in Évian, France, designed "as a musical instrument".

Nestled into a sloping woodland site overlooking Lake Geneva, La Source Vive is a 490-seat chamber music hall situated next to Patrick Bouchain's existing 1993 concert hall La Grange au Lac.

Designed to complement the existing venue, La Source Vive provides a dedicated space for chamber music rehearsals, performances and recordings, while the restored 1,000-seat timber hall La Grange au Lac continues to host large-scale orchestral performances.

Together, the two halls form part of Les Mélèzes, a cultural complex encompassing music and performing arts, founded by French philanthropist Aline Foriel-Destezet.

Achieving high-quality acoustics was the central idea guiding the design of La Source Vive, influencing decisions about the building's geometry and material palette.

Philippe Chiambaretti and Patrick Bouchain worked alongside acoustician Albert Xu to "design the building as a musical instrument", exploring how its form, materials and finishes could influence sound quality.

Read:

Open Architecture unveils rock-like concert hall in a valley outside Beijing

The design process involved acoustic sketches, digital modelling, simulations and repeated on-site testing during construction.

PCA-Stream also developed a digital twin of the project to monitor and refine the hall's acoustic behaviour at different stages.

La Source Vive is set across three volumes – a glazed foyer, the domed concert hall and a separate backstage building containing dressing rooms.

By positioning the project within an existing clearing, the architects aimed to minimise the impact on the woodland site, while enhancing biodiversity through planting more than 150 trees and 200 shrubs alongside landscape studio Coloco.

Linking the old and new halls, the glazed foyer was rebuilt and expanded to include a bar, ticketing area and timber terrace. Rainwater collected beneath the terrace is reused to irrigate the surrounding landscape.

From the foyer, visitors pass through a rock-cut passage before entering a lobby that opens onto the auditorium.

Housed within a domed "partially-buried shell", the concert hall is clad with pre-patinated copper tiles which catch and reflect light, and are designed to weather over time to blend into the surrounding woodland.

Structurally, the concert hall is formed of an acoustic concrete shell wrapped with a second timber frame beneath the copper roof.

Inside, the 490-seat auditorium combines elements of the rectangular "shoebox" concert hall with the more contemporary "vineyard" model, placing audiences on terraced seating around the performers.

The studio opted for a pared-back material palette of concrete, raw plaster, timber and leather throughout.

Curved plaster walls are sculpted with undulating grooves that project up to eight centimetres at audience level, helping to diffuse and reflect sound. Above the stage, a bespoke aluminium canopy was designed to further optimise acoustics.

Solid rose beech timber beams were used for the stage backdrop and flooring, while custom-made dusty orange leather benches are arranged asymmetrically around the stage to create a closer relationship between audience and performers.

An oculus in the ceiling draws natural light inside, fitted with a blackout screen that allows the space to be darkened when required.

Alongside chamber-music performances, La Source Vive accommodates theatre, dance and literary readings, as well as a recording studio space. There are also spaces for workshops, exhibitions and lectures.

A separate volume upslope from the concert hall contains dressing rooms and backstage facilities. Clad in larch and clapboard, its base is made from recycled stone. Elsewhere, stone from the nearby Meillerie quarry was also used for landscaped rockwork.

Other concert halls recently featured on Dezeen include a University of Oxford performing arts centre set around a four-storey atrium by Hopkins Architects and a trio of rectangular red-brick music buildings for MIT by SANAA.

item.content:encoded:
A flat-pack wardrobe that can be assembled with a single Allen key and a concrete bench made of clam shells feature in this roundup of furniture and lighting, spotted by Dezeen's design team over the past month.

ReFrame by Becca Panter

This flat-pack wardrobe by design graduate Becca Panter took home no less than three different awards at this year's New Designers showcase.

The project was born from the discovery that one furniture piece in student halls tends to break above all others: the built-in chipboard wardrobe, which is usually completely unrepairable and mostly ends up in a skip when it is inevitably damaged.

Panter's alternative, made entirely from folded steel for easy recycling, can be assembled and disassembled with a single Allen key and proves that just because furniture is affordable and flat-packed doesn't mean it can't be demounted, repaired and recycled.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by JERMAINE GALLACHER (@jermainegallacher)

Lamps by City Girls

City Girls is an anonymous London design duo causing a stir with its one-of-a-kind lamps made from a mishmash of found treasures.

The professional scavengers leave no stone unturned when sourcing reclaimed materials to transform into lighting – from lace trim, coat hangers and bakelite found across eBay, Facebook Marketplace, and even on the side of the road.

Each lamp is finished as a "city girl" in her own right, affectionately named things like Zoe, Pamela and Jean to give the pieces distinct identities.

The lighting was recently displayed in an exhibition curated by Jermaine Gallacher at the Ragged School in London Bridge, which concluded in July.

Screwssssss stool by Matteo Voisin

For fans of Mikael Axelsson's wood-clamp IKEA stool (guilty as charged), French designer Matteo Voisin has delivered a whole furniture collection that builds on the idea of designing objects to playfully communicate their function.

His most distilled and successful take on the theme is the Screwssssss stool – three identical oak boards held together by colourful, oversized hex nuts to signal that the piece can be easily dismantled, repaired and understood by its owner.

Barefoot Table by Kilzi

Barcelona brand Kilzi sought to capture a sense of "motion held in balance" with Barefoot Table, which was designed with playfully slanted legs to look as if they are moving.

Crafted from solid dyed chestnut, the dining table was created as "an ode to the quiet movement that exists even in moments of stillness", according to studio founder Jorge Suárez-Kilzi.

Heimatlos Chair

A trio of interlocking components makes up this dining chair by the emerging Berlin- and Frankfurt-based Em Ef Studio.

The studio painstakingly 3D-printed grooved layers of biodegradable polylactic acid (PLA) to create the seating, which was designed with an ornate back to recall traditional handcrafted furniture despite the contemporary process.

The result is a smart meeting of past and present design languages.

Othko Lamp by Minjae Kim

New York designer Minjae Kim wrapped two sheets of beautifully translucent fibreglass around a central bulb to create this pendant lighting.

A subtle layer of paint was applied to the inner sheet, creating a ghostly outline on the facade of the lamp. When illuminated, you could be forgiven for thinking that a couple of ice-cold negronis were trapped inside the lamp itself – an illusion that makes for a particularly pleasing design.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Emily Savill (@limeydesign)

Lopsy Lily stool by Emily Savill

So far, the design of posture-improving seats has left much to be desired, usually resembling a kind of cross between sex furniture and medieval torture devices.

Kingston University graduate Emily Savill has delivered a rather more elegant take on the theme with her Lopsy Lily stool. Perched on a circular base and an angled "hoof" cast from recycled aluminium, it subconsciously forces the user to engage their core, improve their posture and maintain lower-body movement to reduce pain and stiffness.

Clam Crete bench by Sami Kimberley

Regenerative designer Sami Kimberley has given invasive Golden Clam shells that she collected from the Thames a second life – crushing them up to make more sustainable concrete and forming them into multi-purpose building blocks.

These blocks can be adapted to fulfil a menagerie of different functions, as a planter, a bench or an entire shelving system, using only readily available materials.

By inviting interaction, the project hopes to demonstrate how materials can help us rebuild a closer relationship to the places we call home and the ecosystems that sustain us.

item.content:encoded:
British designer Beth Morgan Lundie has developed a refillable skincare dispenser that lets users combine different ingredients to create a bespoke formula at home and "bypass the need for toxic additives".

The Meld system was Morgan Lundie's graduation project from London design school Central Saint Martins and earned her the PriestmanGoode Rising Star Award at this year's New Designers showcase.

It consists of a digital platform that enables users to create their own skincare formulas, together with a physical dispenser that combines the ingredients at the point of use.

The system aims to facilitate the co-development of products and improve ingredient transparency, as well as eliminate the need for additives that are commonly used in the skincare industry to increase shelf life.

Studies suggest that more than 60 per cent of cosmetics currently contain preservatives such as parabens, which have been shown to interfere with the body's natural hormones.

As awareness of this issue grows, many consumers are seeking natural alternatives and greater clarity about the ingredients they are putting on their bodies.

"I was fascinated by the disconnect between rituals of personal care and the harsh reality that they could be slowly deteriorating our physical health," the designer told Dezeen.

"I wanted to develop a solution that tackled skincare consumption end-to-end," she added. "Not only was it necessary to rethink the packaging materiality, but to completely bypass the need for toxic additives."

Her Meld concept invites users to create a profile and recommends personalised products based on a series of questions about their current routines, concerns and skin type.

Its digital interface outlines the properties of each formula, along with the natural ingredients it contains and the outcomes users can expect.

The platform includes an option to update the formula to improve its texture, scent, hydration, weight or intensity in response to changes in the user's skin over time.

"By championing ingredient literacy and continuous adaptation to personal needs, the service enables people to better connect with their products and skin health," Morgan Lundie explained.

Read:

Consent Soap provides sex education for people with learning disabilities

Formulas are ordered as a collection of individual ingredients delivered in biodegradable cartridges that can be composted after use.

The cartridges are loaded into a dispenser that was designed for prolonged reuse, made from stainless steel, aluminium, earthenware ceramic and rubber.

It pumps ingredients out in carefully dosed quantities onto a removable mixing lid, which allows users to combine them manually before applying the finished formula.

The device features simple, intuitive shapes and robust materials, including ceramic, stainless steel and natural rubber, to ensure it will last a long time.

"Meld reframes skincare as a participatory ritual built for longevity of use," Morgan Lundie explained

"Creating a feeling of soft tactility was important to the overall experience of the dispenser," she added. "The lid is curved to swipe the contents out with your finger, and the ceramic casing is chamfered for subtle grip."

"Because longevity was also integral to the design language, the resulting form is intentionally simple for efficient cleaning. so that each component can be sterilised in the dishwasher for safe continued use."

Morgan Lundie said she hopes Meld can act as a blueprint for positive changes in the cosmetics industry by promoting a more transparent approach while fostering a sense of personal connection and ritual engagement to the skincare experience.

Other innovations featured at New Designers this year included Safaa Fojdar's portable device for removing creases from clothing on the go.

Another Central Saint Martins graduate, Audrey Levy, recently designed a fuzzy fridge grown from bacteria.

The images are courtesy of Beth Morgan Lundie.

item.content:encoded:
Japanese minimalism has informed the interiors of this light-filled Italian restaurant in Montreal, designed by locally based Ivy Studio with its first in-house designed chairs.

Located on the ground level of a Downtown high-rise residential tower, Minnibar utilises the 20-foot (6-metre) ceilings, corner aspect and almost square floor plan to its advantage.

Ivy Studio left the building's structure entirely visible, and only added elements where functionally necessary – using the principles of Japanese minimalism as a guide.

"Minnibar embraces its raw shell," said the studio. "Exposed base-building elements – including the naturally sealed concrete floor, formidable concrete columns, walls, and the ceiling slab – are left untouched."

The kitchen, bar and pizza counter are housed within an enclosed central core, allowing the cafe and restaurant spaces to flow openly around the perimeter.

Morning patrons have easy access from the entrance to the cafe counter, which is clad in monolithic, cream-colored stone with a leather finish.

As it continues into the space, the counter drops in height and is replaced with an omakase-style ledge crafted from white oak.

Opposite, a black shelf runs along the windows to provide additional bar dining space, accompanied by circular white stools.

"The design employs a strict monochromatic palette, playing with off-white and grey shades punctuated by sharp black integrations," said Ivy Studio.

"To give the minimalist aesthetic a profound sense of depth, the design introduces subtle, highly tactile finishes: hand-plastered walls, heavily textured stones, opaque stained wood grains, and translucent textiles."

The main dining space features freestanding black tables for flexibility, which are typically arranged in a symmetrical layout around an adjustable glowing artwork on the back wall.

Several custom furnishings, which represent "a study in contrast and craftsmanship," are installed throughout the restaurant.

These include Ivy Studio's first in-house designed chair, which features softly curved legs and a delicate backrest – all crafted from ash wood and stained soft yellow.

The sculptural, stainless steel DJ booth was created in collaboration with local shop Procedures Industries and is equipped with built-in vinyl players.

Read:

Ivy Studio designs "bold and glamorous" Montreal restaurant

Triangular details recur throughout, including in the stainless steel bar counter footrest, windows into the wine cellar, wall-mounted light fixtures and millwork.

Rice-paper screens help to shade the interiors from bright sunlight and also form acoustic buffers across the ceiling.

"Minnibar successfully harmonises the gritty, raw shell of downtown Montreal's urban architecture with the refined, atmospheric principles of Japanese minimalism," said the studio.

"By contrasting heavy, exposed concrete with custom monolithic furniture, dynamic lighting, and an uncompromising dedication to sound and culinary craft, the space transcends the traditional restaurant model to offer a truly immersive, day-to-night destination."

Ivy Studio has completed multiple restaurants across Montreal, including the "bold and glamorous" Limousine, the marble-filled Hayat, and Piatti, which was resurrected after a fire.

The firm's portfolio also includes an indoor golf club, an ad agency in a converted bank and a creative hub with a "work in progress" aesthetic.

The photography is by Alex Lesage.

item.content:encoded:
Spanish studio NUA Arquitectures has completed Casa Juià, a farmhouse in Catalonia that draws on the craftsmanship of the surrounding region.

Located in the village of Juià, at the foot of the Gavarres mountain range in Spain, the 283-square-metre home comprises three parallel wings wrapped in porches and galleries.

Casa Juià reinterprets the region's traditional farmhouse typology, known as masia, and also takes cues from neighbouring structures, local roof forms and the site's original terrain.

"The project is conceived as a contemporary interpretation of the traditional Catalan farmhouse," NUA arquitectures co-founder Arnau Tiñena told Dezeen.

Casa Juià was built for a family of five who returned to rural life after several years in a city.

The house stands opposite a traditional rural farmhouse on Mas Nadal, a road on the edge of Juià, at the transition between the village and a forest of cork, pine and oak.

"Its central idea is to inhabit the transition between the village and the forest, creating an architecture that is deeply rooted in its context while expressing a clear contemporary identity," said studio partner Ferran Tiñena.

"The house mirrors an existing farmhouse and reinterprets it in typology, moving away from romanticism and literal imitation," added Arnau.

The farmhouse's layout, materials and handcrafted construction methods were chosen to celebrate local knowledge, while also tending towards more contemporary design.

It is arranged as three parallel, two-storey wings that give the building a clear order within the rougher surrounding terrain.

"The linear structure allows the dwelling to unfold as a sequence of interconnected spaces that extend toward the landscape," said Ferran.

A staircase leads from the garden up to a double-height entrance, which opens onto the ground-floor living areas, with bedrooms above.

Read:

Madras Spaces creates rural Indian home using "only what was necessary"

On the ground floor, the interiors extend onto a covered porch, while upstairs they lead onto a gallery – opening the house to scenic views. The staggered arrangement of these porches and galleries is intended to evoke the layout and passive climate control found in the local farmhouses.

The east-west axis of the site is left open to maximise sunlight, cross-ventilation and views over the fields, while the enclosed north-south axis borders the forest and adjacent properties, and features solid, thermally efficient walls.

"The design is entirely shaped by the specific conditions of the site, reinforcing the idea of the house as a passage through the land," said Arnau.

"Equally significant is the careful framing of views, which establishes a constant dialogue with the surrounding landscape."

Casa Juià's material palette was chosen for its texture and durability. Timber, ceramic and lime mortar are used throughout the project, each locally sourced and central to the local construction industry.

"All three of the primary materials used in Casa Juià are natural, locally sourced materials with a low environmental footprint, deeply rooted in the region's construction culture," said Arnau.

Timber is used for the house's floor beams, joinery and custom-designed furniture, while ceramic forms the roof covering and protective waterproof cladding on the facades, as well as the flooring and wall finishes inside.

Lime mortar glazes the exterior facade and many of the interior walls.

"Materiality plays a fundamental role in the identity of the project," said Arnau. "It celebrates the honesty of construction rather than concealing it."

Local craftsmanship shaped the handmade finishes and custom-built elements throughout, which were designed to preserve the imperfections and character of the structure rather than smooth them away.

"Materials are not only a construction system but also an expression of local culture, craftsmanship and time," Ferran continued. "By prioritising local materials, collaborating with regional craftspeople and supporting traditional building techniques, the project reinforces local knowledge and contributes to the circular economy."

Other farmhouses recently featured on Dezeen include a Highlands house with blackened-larch extension by Loader Monteith, a 1970s timber-and-brick farmhouse by Bastiaan Jongerius Architecten and a 19th-century Somerset by Forgeworks.

The photography is by José Hevia.

A large multi-generational home in India and a low-lying stone farmhouse in rural Scotland are among the mix of residences in this eclectic edition of Dezeen's houses of the month.

Also on the list of the five most popular houses featured on Dezeen in July are a gridded forest dwelling in the Netherlands, a rammed-earth courtyard house in New Zealand and a stepped home on the Mexican coast.

Read on to find out more about Dezeen readers' favourite houses this month:

Dulnain, Scotland, by Loader Monteith

The most popular house on Dezeen this month was Dulnain, a three-bedroom family home in the Scottish Highlands.

Designed by Loader Monteith, the project involved rebuilding a derelict farmhouse and adding a blackened-larch extension that divides the home into two wings. Approximately 90 per cent of the building's original granite blocks were repurposed for the build.

Find out more about Dulnain ›

Forest Villa MB, the Netherlands, by Tom Kneepkens

A gridded timber roof overhangs Forest Villa MB, which architect Tom Kneepkens designed to feel connected to its woodland site in the Netherlands.

The roof incorporates openings through which trees can grow, while large expanses of glazing allow plenty of views out to nature.

"Rather than imposing itself on the landscape, the architecture adapts to the natural environment, allowing the built structure and the existing vegetation to coexist," said Kneepkens.

Find out more about Forest Villa MB ›

Double Courtyard House, New Zealand, by Roberts Gray Architects

Rammed earth was used to form the low-slung Double Courtyard House, designed Roberts Gray Architects on a sand dune near Auckland.

Within its heavy walls are two contrasting courtyards – one shaded and one exposed to sun – around which the living spaces are organised, giving the home its name.

Find out more about Double Courtyard House ›

Casa Diez Pies, Mexico, by Studio Font

Casa Diez Pies was conceived as a series of stepped terraces, supported by 10 chunky concrete columns, which descend a coastal cliff in Mazunte.

The 10 supports, which give the home its name Casa Diez Pies or Ten-Foot House, were designed to minimise the impact on the site while creating spaces for staircases, bathrooms and storage spaces.

Find out more about Casa Diez Pies ›

Splitscape Residence, India, by SpaceDNA

This multi-generational house in India is organised across split-level floors and an orange staircase, encased by facades of perforated steel screens.

The jaali-like screens filter light into the home, including a triple-height living space at its heart, while allowing natural ventilation and creating a sense of openness.

"The interior design was intentionally kept minimal so that spatial experience, light and materiality could take centre stage," the studio told Dezeen.

item.content:encoded:
This week on Dezeen, we unveiled a pair of slides that heat up and vibrate feet to help athlete's recover.

Created by sportswear company Nike and health technology company Hyperice, the slides contain a device in their straps that can heat and massage the top of feet.

Continuing our Future Stadium series we investigated why stadiums are becoming more outlandish and impactful.

To conclude the series, we rounded up the world's record-breaking stadiums including, the biggest and the most expensive.

item.content:encoded:
New York City studio Martin Hopp Architect has completed a building with a mass-timber structure for a school in Hempstead, New York, prioritising healthy living spaces and materials on a tight budget.

Evergreen Charter School opened in 2025 on a suburban site on Long Island in New York state. The K-12 school comprises 89,000 square feet (8,270 square metres) of conditioned space and 106,000 square feet (9,850 square metres) of non-conditioned space and prioritises healthy, resilient learning environments.

"From the outset, we focused on creating high-performance spaces filled with daylight, fresh air and natural materials – environments that would actively support students' wellbeing and concentration," said studio founder Martin Hopp.

"With a very limited budget, we made a deliberate decision to pursue a 'most from least' approach."

The studio invested in performance with a mass timber structure, efficient systems, durable materials and flexible classrooms that can change over time to meet the school's needs.

"The ambition was not spectacle, but generosity – to demonstrate that even under tight constraints, a school building can be uplifting, responsible and deeply supportive of learning," Hopp said.

The limited footprint prompted the team to divide the building into two volumes with a slot carved through the massing that allows daylight to reach deep into the plan.

The circulation spine aligns with the junction of the two volumes, allowing cross views across the five floors.

"In this way, the layout balances efficiency with environmental performance," the studio said.

"The compact footprint maximizes usable space on the site, while the split massing strategy prioritizes daylight, ventilation and a strong sense of spatial organization for students and staff."

The whole school was designed around a classroom model that prioritised natural light, acoustics, thermal comfort and indoor air quality.

In addition to the structure that reduces the building's embodied carbon, mass timber is used throughout the entire building as the finish material, adding warmth, texture, and visual calm to the environment.

On the exterior, timber shading devices run in long fins up the primary facade, providing a warm, natural contrast to the grey cementitious panels. Above the upper enclosed floor, a timber pergola topped with solar arrays shades the rooftop soccer pitch.

Inside, the ceilings of the classrooms, gymnasium and cafeteria are partially exposed mass timber, while acoustic ceiling panels help maintain noise levels.

Read:

AMMA completes mass-timber modular school "that breathes" in Barbados

The project is tracking toward LEED Platinum certification with a range of passive and active sustainability strategies.

"Together, these passive and active systems reinforce the project's core ambition," the studio said. "To create a high-performance learning environment that reduces operational costs while supporting student health and environmental awareness."

Mass timber architecture has spread to education architecture over the last several years with projects like the University of Arkansas' architecture and design school by Grafton Architects, a treehouse-like social hub at Harvard University by Studio Gang and a lantern-like research centre for the University of Toronto by Montgomery Sisam Architects.

item.content:encoded:
A horizontal glass skybridge connects residential and office skyscrapers at this project by Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados in São Paulo to preserve the "individual reading of each tower while simultaneously reinforcing their unity".

Located in São Paulo as part of the larger Eixo Platina mixed-use development by developer Porte Engenharia e Urbanism, the Almagah 227 skyscrapers were designed to respond to demand for commercial and corporate spaces in the city's East Zone.

Almagah 227 consists of one 25-floor residential tower and one 27-floor office tower. They are linked by the skybridge on the 13th through 14th floor, which contrasts the towers' warm, porcelain facade with dark glazing.

"By articulating the two buildings, the bridge preserves the individual reading of each tower while simultaneously reinforcing their unity as a single ensemble," said Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados."It expands the functional integration of the development and consolidates the identity of the complex."

The buildings also stand on a broad, glass base that is clad in the same dark glazing as the bridge above. At the bottom of the residential skyscraper, the platform runs into a large pool deck and recreation area.

Along the entirety of the ground floor, the base contains commercial spaces, while the 2nd and 3rd floors contain open-plan coworking areas.

The bridge itself contains corporate programming, along with a restaurant, while the residential tower includes "compact" and studio apartments.

The studio said the facade was constructed using a ventilated facade system, which contains a small gap between its porcelain cladding and the masonry structure.

Read:

Nitsche Arquitetos integrates timber kiosks into São Paulo metro station renovations

Constant air circulating through this space removes "approximately 20 per cent" of absorbed heat, according to the team, while the system also allowed expedited construction time, reduced waste generation and "less maintenance".

As part of the broader Eixo Platina masterplan, the area is intended to provide mixed-use programming in São Paulo's dense East Zone. It contains several skyscrapers along a broad strip in the city, some of which have already been completed.

"Almagah 227 reflects the core principles of Eixo Platina by incorporating programmatic diversity, strong integration with its surroundings and architectural solutions that enhance the city."

"The complex stems from the same principle that structures the entire masterplan: bringing housing, work and leisure into closer proximity, reducing daily commutes and qualifying the urban environment through diverse and connected infrastructure," said the studio.

Elsewhere in the city, Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados completed a skyscraper with porcelain and wood cladding, while FGMF Arquitetos completed a pixelated skyscraper in the Pinheiros district.

item.content:encoded:
British studio Charles Gillespie Architecture has completed The Linhay, a family house in rural Somerset wrapped by a deep concrete colonnade that provides sheltered nesting spaces for birds.

Designed by the studio's founder Charles Gillespie for himself and his young family, the house draws on the traditional linhay – an agricultural barn found across Somerset and Devon with a distinctive open-fronted form.

Rather than recreating the historic building type, the studio translated its defining characteristics into a full-length colonnade formed from precast concrete columns.

Behind this row of precast concrete columns is a sheltered terrace, which leads directly to main living spaces through large glazed openings. The recessed facade blocks high summer sun and admits lower winter light.

The cylindrical columns reference the historic linhay barns, where rounded supports made it easier for livestock to pass through the open-fronted structures, while giving the facade a regular rhythm.

Bird and bat boxes, bee bricks and nesting spaces are integrated into this area, allowing it to double as habitat for local wildlife.

"The colonnade gives the house its identity, controls sunlight, extends the living space and provides shelter for wildlife," Gillespie told Dezeen.

"Environmental performance, biodiversity and architectural character do not need to be separate ambitions."

Gillespie recalled that the distinctive structure initially sparked some confusion among neighbours during construction.

"The precast colonnade was erected quite early during the build," Gillespie said. "I'd say our neighbours had a bit of a shock, perhaps with the fear we were building some kind of Greek revival building in the middle of a field!"

Read:

Forgeworks revamps Somerset farmhouse with low-lying stone extension

The two-storey home sits on West Farm in Babcary as part of an intergenerational development that also includes Highlands, a second house for Gillespie's parents.

Together, the buildings replace a collection of former agricultural outbuildings while allowing three generations of the same family to live independently on the same site.

Gillespie described the arrangement as a "family campus", with the two houses connected by shared gardens and daily routines while remaining separate homes.

From the approach, the Linhay resembles a deliberately simple pitched-roof farmhouse combining pale stone with vertical timber cladding.

A lower wing with an intensive green roof extends into the former farmyard, creating the impression that part of the surrounding field has been folded over the building.

Inside, the home is organised around an open-plan kitchen, dining and play space that projects into the garden, giving it views in three directions across meadow planting and surrounding fields.

Exposed timber ceiling beams, lime-plastered walls, polished concrete floors and cherry timber joinery create a restrained material palette, punctuated by a pink pigmented concrete staircase.

Timber was sourced from the nearby Stourhead estate, while the stone came from a quarry seven miles from the site.

Around the house, meadow planting, an orchard and pollinator-friendly species replace areas of former hardstanding.

The green roof and surrounding planting are intended to strengthen biodiversity across the farmstead.

The all-electric home combines passive environmental strategies with an air-source heat pump, mechanical ventilation with heat recovery and rooftop photovoltaic panels.

Charles Gillespie Architecture was founded by Gillespie in 2024 in Castle Cary, Somerset. The studio focuses on homes and rural projects, with The Linhay and the neighbouring Highlands house among its first completed works.

Other British houses recently featured on Dezeen include the brick-clad Skylark home, for which House of EM referenced mid-century design principles, and Westview Cottage in Dungeness, which Hollaway Studio completed with a monochrome palette.

item.content:encoded:
Certification company Bureau Veritas has launched the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard, a voluntary verification scheme that determines a building's carbon performance.

Now open for submissions, the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard assesses net-zero claims of buildings against an industry-agreed definition, aiming to minimise greenwashing.

New buildings, existing buildings and retrofit projects can be entered voluntarily to the standard, which grants a Net Zero Carbon Aligned verification to buildings that meet the set criteria.

Verification requires 12 months of in-use building data

Buildings submitted to the scheme will be assessed by Bureau Veritas based on 12 months of in-use energy data and as-built upfront embodied-carbon data.

To be verified as Net Zero Carbon Aligned, buildings must remove on-site fossil fuels, generate on-site renewable energy and minimise the upfront embodied carbon and measured in-use energy consumption.

Offsets cannot be used to meet any of the required limits, but can be considered to tackle residual carbon when mandatory requirements are met.

Standard "marks a pivotal shift in the industry"

Bureau Veritas hopes that providing a set standard for net zero in the building industry will build credibility in carbon claims, shifting the focus from design-stage modelling data to in-use performance.

"The launch of verification under the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard marks a pivotal shift in the industry, moving from predicted outcomes to measured, independently verified in-use performance," said Bureau Veritas vice president Antoine Giros.

"As verification administrator, Bureau Veritas will ensure that net-zero claims are accurate, reliable, and backed by rigorous assessment," he continued. "Our role is to provide independent expertise in building performance and carbon assessment, to give investors, occupiers, and stakeholders genuine confidence in building performance."

"With nearly 200 years of credibility in testing, inspection and certification, we're proud to support the industry's transition towards a low-carbon future."

Read:

"It's time to see all those circular economy strategies for what they are"

Prior to final verification, buildings can undergo a verified check at the practical completion stage to gauge whether they are on track to meet the standards when in use.

Bureau Veritas also provides a carbon performance evaluation for buildings that do not meet all the requirements for Net Zero Carbon Aligned verification, to track their decarbonisation progress.

"It is now only a matter of time before the first buildings are verified as Net Zero Carbon Aligned," said UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard CEO Katie Jackson-Clements.

"These front-runners will represent environmental leadership within the UK built environment industry and pave the way for many more verifications to follow."

Sustainable buildings that have recently featured on Dezeen include a net-zero campus in Washington for the American Institute of Architects and a house in the Hamptons designed to be net-positive-energy.

In this week's comments update, readers are discussing Yano Aoyama Architecture Design's public toilet for the Tobe Zoological Park in Ehime Prefecture, Japan.

Comprising a pair of sculpted concrete blocks topped by a naturally curved cedar roof, the design of the public bathroom cubicles draws from the zoo's wooded surroundings.

"Simple, beautiful forms"

Commenters were on the same page, doling out high praise for the Japanese public toilet.

"This is powerful, correct, elegant, vaguely historical, well-made... I could go on," wrote Ben.

Pa Varreon agreed, saying, "Very much elegant. I would almost travel to Japan to visit and use these facilities."

"Simple, beautiful forms," remarked Steve Hassler. "Thanks for this."

Andy Enock wrote, "Japan takes this seriously; they have some brilliant designs."

"It is magnificent and beautiful, I wish we could have something like this in the USA," wrote Joaquin. "Pay here is not the same as pee here, people," he added.

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion ›

"The 90s called and asked for their clunky designs back"

Another story gaining traction this week was the North Tower skyscraper in Chicago by architecture studio SOM, which features a series of cascading terraces.

"I actually like the 80s throwback to geometric play," said Frank Lloyd Wrong.

In accord, Layla wrote, "This is a great contrast to the confused hodge-podge of residential buildings on the other side of the river. Looks good to me!"

"This is much more interesting than the typical glass box condo tower with wafer balconies," said Fremp. "It's like a new take on a classic art deco massing. Great addition to the Chicago skyline."

"Sleek and sane!" said Blau.

Other commenters weren't so keen.

"The 90s called and asked for their clunky designs back," wrote RK. "'Tired skyscraper' would have been a more apt article headline."

Luc Helterbrand said, "In person this building appears very heavy and clumsy. Disappointing addition to the skyline of this great city."

"It's not finished, but I doubt it will look better when it is," wrote This is not Hank in agreement.

Have you had your say yet? Join the discussion ›

"1970s inspired tower with beaver chew"

A project that intrigued readers was the Atlassian Central skyscraper in Sydney by SHoP Architects and BVN Architecture, which has become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

"Appropriate then that the shape resembles a tree about to be felled," said Jim Angrabright.

Milton Welch responded to this, calling it a "1970s inspired tower with beaver chew".

"Intrigued by the structure, but also the final enclosure," wrote JZ. "As far as high-rises go, it appears to have its own unique, coherent and tasteful resolution."

"Looking good," agreed Matthew. "But those slanted glazings are providing fantastic ledges for pigeons."

Though replies were overwhelmingly positive, some commenters expressed doubts.

"Where is the heavy timber shipped from? Do they consider this travel distance in the calculations of the amount of embodied energy?" asked DEvODA. "Sometimes these things are all show and no real benefit."

"What staggers me is the sheer volume of the voids around the intriguing internal wooden floors and walls," wrote John. "What purpose do these spaces serve?"

Just as unimpressed, Tom Roberts said, "Who cares what it is made of, it is an ugly and unbalanced design."
