item.content:encoded:
A bridge with towers informed by a hockey slapshot has opened to public traffic between the United States and Canada after more than seven years of construction, decades of planning and a contentious back-and-forth with the federal government.

Named after Canadian-born Detroit Red Wings hockey player Gordie Howe, the bridge stretches over the Detroit River between the city of Detroit and Windsor, Canada.

It is "the first new crossing between Ontario and Michigan in over 60 years", according to the organising body the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority (WDBA).

WDBA coordinated the project, while design was led by AECOM.

On either side, the project includes border inspection facilities for travellers, while a toll-free multi-use pedestrian path stretches its length.

In total, it encompasses six bridge lanes, 16 toll lanes and 60 Canada and US inspection lanes.

Upon its completion, its main span is "the longest of any cable-stayed bridge in North America" according to WDBA, and its 720-foot-tall (220-metre) towers are among the tallest structures in the region.

AECOM bridge architect Erik Behrens, who was one of the first to drive across the bridge during opening ceremonies on 27 July 2026, said the towers' curves were designed to recall the arc of Howe's hockey stick mid-slapshot.

"The bridge's aesthetic appeal lies in the extreme slenderness of its gently curving deck,” said Behrens. "Together with the stay cables, it creates an impression of gravity- defying lightness and transparency."

Along with spanning a major trade route between Michigan and Ontario, the project now includes the largest ports of entry along the Canada-US border, according to the team.

Read:

Finland's longest bridge reaches completion in Helsinki

This has made the project a complex and political saga over the years, following its initial planning stages that started in the 2000s.

Most recently, US president Donald Trump has been attempting to block its opening after demanding that Canada hand over additional ownership of the bridge to the US, detail in a Truth Social post. It's currently jointly owned between Canada and Michigan, although Canada agreed to front the cost for construction.

In an original 2012 crossing deal, the two bodies agreed toll fees would go to Canada once the debt had been recouped; however, amidst Trump's outburst and threat of imposing tariffs, the deal structure is being relitigated.

The drama also caused Canada to disinvite the US from the bridge's opening ceremonies on Friday, 24 July, causing further tension.

However, the WDBA remained committed to opening the bridge to traffic on Monday, and for now, it's in use.

Elsewhere around the world, Finland's longest bridge was completed in Helsinki and Italy's former head of motorways was sentenced to 12 years in prison over a bridge collapse in Genoa.

The photography is courtesy of the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority.

item.dc:creator: Tom Ravenscroft
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Stadiums are becoming more distinctive with clubs and countries using them to attract attention. As part of our Future Stadium series, we look at why stadium design is becoming more icon-focused.

UK-based Heatherwick Studio had never designed a stadium before, so its recent win in the competition to design Birmingham City's stadium – along with its design, which will see the stadium encircled in 12 giant chimneys – surprised many.

"As someone who bid for the Birmingham City stadium, it's fair to say I didn't imagine it as a Victorian factory," ZHA director Jim Heverin told Dezeen in a piece for this series.

The Heatherwick Studio-designed stadium will undoubtedly be distinctive, and it represents a growing trend where the owners of the world's best-known sports teams demand an aesthetically striking, unique structure.

"That's why we were put on the shortlist," Heatherwick Studio partner Eliot Postma told Dezeen.

"They probably knew what they were going to get from a lot of the competitors, and we were a bit of an unknown quantity."

"I haven't seen all of the other designs in the competition, but I wouldn't be surprised if ours was the boldest in its explicit landmark nature."

Increasingly, major sports clubs are huge global brands. Building this brand, along with the commercial capabilities that go with it, is a major part of a club's focus.

"Most clubs nowadays see themselves more as a brand than just as a sports entity, which may have been the situation like in the 70s or 80s when the focus was really 'we gotta win' and 'we're gonna have the greatest team'," GMP Architekten director Martin Glass told Dezeen.

"Nowadays, it's much more multifaceted, so they have to become like lifestyle brands. They earn as much money selling T-shirts as they earn from TV rights."

Real Madrid "wanted to have a statement"

According to Glass, who recently led the €1 billion overhaul of Real Madrid's Estadio Santiago Bernabéu, this change in thinking is having a marked impact on stadium design. While fan experience is still a priority, the need to create an iconic, eye-catching structure is a key part of the brief.

"Real Madrid has a very, very clear vision about the development of their brand, the possibilities and their whole future outlook," he continued.

"For them, it was absolutely clear that they wanted to have a statement that visually reflects their own visions, and so that was, of course, also an important task for us."

UK studio Foster + Partners, which is currently designing stadiums for three of the world's biggest football clubs – a 100,000-seat venue for Manchester United and a joint stadium for AC Milan and Inter Milan to replace the iconic San Siro, echoed this thought.

"The club's aspiration is to have an iconic, never-seen-before, timeless, you know, classic," Foster + Partners senior partner Angus Campbell told Dezeen.

"There's a bit of me that misses the 60s, 70s, 80s stadia"

Historically, many stadiums developed ad hoc over time. This resulted in unique forms, often with stands of different heights and eras surrounding the pitch.

However, throughout the 1980s and 90s, more and more stadiums were developed and built all at once, resulting in cohesive, aesthetically similar bowls. While these stadiums gave all fans consistent, unobstructed views of the pitch, they sometimes lacked the character of older venues.

"There's a bit of me that misses the 60s, 70s, 80s stadia that evolved over time," said Heatherwick Studio's Postma.

"In old stadiums you'd get like the South Stand and Tilton Road End – they'd be built in different periods and would have different characters, so you wouldn't get this completely homogenous appearance," he continued.

"From around the 80s through to now, there's often an incredible internal environment that gets slickly skinned with this sort of contemporary architecture that all too often does feel like a bit generic."

"You can't just copy-paste anymore"

With contemporary stadiums, studios are aiming to retain the high-quality viewing experience, but also create an iconic silhouette without becoming farcical.

"I don't think people are striving for a gimmick, as such," said Populous senior principal Maria Knutsson-Hall. "The fan has more expectations, but the owners also have more expectations, so you know you can't just copy-paste anymore and be the same as others."

"The identity of the building needs to be much more about placemaking than just creating a home for that club."

Read:

File into the Future Stadium

According to Foster + Partners' Campbell, the key to creating an iconic stadium is going beyond wrapping the stadium in a bright or colourful facade and really pushing engineering to be part of the form.

"Many stadiums try to create a unique identity," he said. "But if you try and do it in cladding and materials only, does that have the gravitas to stand the test of time?"

GMP Architekten director Glass gave Wembley Stadium, designed by Foster + Partners and Populous, as an example where "structural necessity" led to the creation of an iconic structure.

"Good architecture should be able to marry the aesthetic quality and the visual iconisation of a building with the actual technical requirements."

"[At Wembley] on one hand, it's a giant arch that holds a bit of roof, some floodlights, but being quality architects, of course, they were able to combine the two features," he continued.

"This is also something that for us as GMP is very important to have – structural necessity solved in a creative way to give it an aesthetic quality."

"We're not designing a jacket that's just arbitrary"

Campbell explained that the innovation seen at Wembley was part of Foster + Partners' design ideology, which is currently being developed in its design of Manchester United's stadium.

"We're not designing a jacket that's just arbitrary," he said. "It comes from an expression of how the stadium is accessed, used and sits within the city."

"With Manchester United, the whole reason is obviously that it has elements of the club's identity in the trident form, but it [the stadium's planned tent-like canopy] also has a functional role of making the stadium bigger than a stadium – extending the envelope to embrace the precinct."

Even though Heatherwick Studio's design for Birmingham City appears at first viewing to be slightly gimmicky, Postma explained that the design also came from a series of "quite logical decisions".

He explained that the fans had already responded to the design and were adopting it into chants.

"The second game after we released the design, there was a new chant going around the stadium of 'we are the chimney boys' – so for us, that's sort of the dream."

"Backlash in using branding or naming rights"

The focus on brand identity is also having another impact, not on the design, but on the naming of stadiums.

As clubs focus more on building their own brand, Populous' Knutsson-Hall predicts that we may see fewer stadiums named after sponsors as clubs consider naming rights as part of a wider branding strategy.

"There's a lot of fatigue, and also a backlash against using branding or naming rights," she said.

"What you do see now, particularly here in the UK, you see Tottenham Hotspur Stadium not a branded name, Fulham Riverside not a branded name, because they have many brands underneath that umbrella," she continued.

"So, the key thing in placemaking is to create an umbrella destination."

While football clubs are utilising stadiums to enhance their brand reach, countries are also commissioning stadiums with the direct aim of drawing attention to their country.

Foster + Partners drew attention to how the stadiums that hosted the past two World Cups provide an insight into how thinking is changing. The 2026 final was hosted in the relatively unrecognisable MetLife Stadium, which opened in 2010, while in 2022 Lusail Stadium, which was built specifically as a symbol for Qatar, hosted the final.

"The World Cup final has just been held in a stadium that I didn't even know what it looked like while the tournament was happening – I had no idea," said Campbell.

"[Whereas] Lusail is an instantly recognisable image," he continued. "The tournament was four years ago and probably no one could tell you what the other stadiums look like – they've forgotten."

Read:

What will the future stadium look like?

Campbell explained that Lusail Stadium was designed not only to host games, but to be a recognisable icon for the tournament.

"Lusail was about creating an identity for a country and a tournament," he said. "Suddenly you've got an audience of three billion watching the World Cup, if you're lucky, over the 10 games, maybe a million people actually got to visit it," he continued.

"We set out to create an emblem for a country and something that could be seen on the TV cameras for the global audience and become something that was identifiable for Lusail as a contemporary city and for the country of Qatar."

This trend looks to be continuing in Saudi Arabia, where a whole host of distinctive-looking stadiums are being built ahead of the World Cup in 2034.

Granite cloaks the sweeping form of Shenzhen Natural History Museum, completed in China by architecture studios 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design.

Now officially open in the Pingshan District, the 100,000-square-metre building was planned as a new cultural landmark for Shenzhen.

It is distinguished by its fluid form that rises from the ground, designed by 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design to evoke nearby rivers and hills.

"Nothing in nature is square," said 3XN founder Kim Herforth Nielsen.

"Nature is amorphous, dynamic, and always in formation. From the beginning, the ambition was to create not a building, but a piece of landscape that had always been there – shaped by local geology, water and time," he continued.

"That idea has been carried all the way from the competition stage to the museum that opens today, a place where the story of our planet is experienced as a physical journey through terrain, light and space."

The design team 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design won a competition to design Shenzhen Natural History Museum in 2020 for a site beside Yanzi Lake. It is the largest natural history museum in southern China.

The museum's sweeping form rises from the ground with a sloping roof and terraces, which allow direct access from ground level to invite "everyday use beyond the threshold of the galleries", the studios said.

Externally, the museum is wrapped in strips of granite with openings intended to appear as though they have been carved within it.

Inside, it is divided across five cone-shaped volumes, linked by cave-like passages and atriums.

The galleries are dedicated to exhibits on natural history, as well as the ecology of Shenzhen and its surrounding region.

Photos of the galleries are yet to be released, but these have been developed with Atelier Brückner and Museum Studio to be "immersive, media‑rich environments". There is also a range of specimens on display alongside large‑scale installations.

Read:

Mecanoo completes rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi

"Shenzhen Natural History Museum is designed to interpret the laws of natural evolution and present the geographies of Shenzhen in a global ecological perspective," said the museum director Nan Zhaoxu.

"It brings together collections and research that trace 4.6 billion years of Earth’s history, but it is the architecture that makes this story tangible," he continued.

"By turning the museum into a living educational landscape – from the roof park to the cone‑shaped galleries – it allows visitors from Shenzhen and around the world to experience science, nature and place as one continuous journey that is specific to its place."

Elsewhere in Shenzhen, Urbanus recently designed a colourful school modelled on Hakka walled houses while MAD created a trio of "cloud buildings" for the Tencent headquarters.

Another natural history museum recently featured on Dezeen is the white, rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, which Mecanoo completed on Saadiyat Island.

The photography is by Adam Mørk.

item.content:encoded:
The long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, designed by the late architect Frank Gehry, is set to open its doors in December.

In a statement released today, Abu Dhabi's department of culture and tourism said the museum will open on Saadiyat Island on 11 December 2026, officially becoming the largest of the four Guggenheim outposts.

It is currently under construction in the island's cultural district, for which Gehry also designed the recently revealed Dar al Funoon Abu Dhabi performing arts venue.

Photos reveal building's clashing forms

"Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will open its doors on 11 December 2026, further strengthening Abu Dhabi's position as a leading global capital for the arts," read the department's statement.

"Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is a museum of modern and contemporary art and will be a space for encounter and exchange, promoting a more connected and diverse global community through art."

Plans for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi were first revealed in 2006, with construction beginning in 2011. Works were then suspended for several years, before restarting in 2019.

The building will be distinguished by its giant clashing forms, revealed in a new set of photos released today. These will contain galleries of varying heights and styles.

Alongside these galleries will be a centre for art and technology, as well as children's facilities, archives, a library and a conservation laboratory.

Once open, Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will be operated by the Solomon R Guggenheim Foundation and Abu Dhabi's department of culture and tourism.

Gehry found project "truly thrilling"

In 2021, it was revealed that the museum was scheduled for completion in 2025. At the time, Gehry described the project as "truly thrilling".

"I hope that this building is embraced by the people of the UAE and that this work will endure as a landmark for the country for many years to come," he said.

Read:

Abu Dhabi reveals plans for Frank Gehry-designed performing arts venue

Guggenheim Abu Dhabi's completion will follow the recent openings of other landmark cultural institutions on the island, including Jean Nouvel's Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2017 and Zayed National Museum by Foster + Partners in December 2025.

At 42,000 square metres, it will overtake Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in size.

Other landmark buildings by Gehry, who passed away in December, include Walt Disney Concert Hall and Luna Arles.

The photos are courtesy of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.
